title: Integrality of an algebra element is detected at every base prime
statement: Let $R\to A$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings and let $a\in A$. For each prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$ (a proper ideal such that $uv\in\mathfrak p$ implies $u\in\mathfrak p$ or $v\in\mathfrak p$), put $S_{\mathfrak p}=R\setminus\mathfrak p$, $R_{\mathfrak p}=S_{\mathfrak p}^{-1}R$, and $A_{\mathfrak p}=S_{\mathfrak p}^{-1}A$, with denominators acting through $R\to A$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Then $a$ is integral over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] if and only if $a/1\in A_{\mathfrak p}$ is integral over $R_{\mathfrak p}$ for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of $R$. No injectivity, domain, finiteness, or nonzero-ring hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: For the forward implication, take a monic relation $a^n+\sum_{i<n}\varphi(r_i)a^i=0$ in $A$. Applying $A\to A_{\mathfrak p}$ gives the same monic relation with coefficients $r_i/1\in R_{\mathfrak p}$, proving integrality at every prime. For the converse, first dispose of $R=0$: the unital map forces $A=0$, and $a=0$ satisfies the monic polynomial $X$. Henceforth assume $R\ne0$.

source.place: Tag 034K (lemma-integral-closure-stalks), forward implication; Tag 00GI (definition-integral), including the zero-ring case.

proof.text:
Assume the prime-local integrality hypothesis and put $B=\{\sum_{i=0}^{m}\varphi(b_i)a^i:m\ge0,\ b_i\in R\}\subseteq A$, the $R$-subalgebra generated by $a$. Fix a prime $\mathfrak p$ and a monic relation $a^n+\sum_{i<n}(r_i/s_i)a^i=0$ in $A_{\mathfrak p}$, with $n\ge1$ and $s_i
otin\mathfrak p$. Put $d=\prod_{i<n}s_i$ and $d_i=\prod_{j<n,\ j
e i}s_j$, so $s_i d_i=d$. The element $c=\varphi(d)a^n+\sum_{i<n}\varphi(r_i d_i)a^i\in B$ has image zero in $A_{\mathfrak p}$. The localization equality criterion gives $u
otin\mathfrak p$ with $\varphi(u)c=0$ in $A$, hence also in the actual subring $B$. Set $f=ud
otin\mathfrak p$. Both $u$ and $d$ are units in $R_f$, since $u^{-1}=d/f$ and $d^{-1}=u/f$. Dividing the displayed equality by $ud$ in $B_f$ gives $(a/1)^n+\sum_{i<n}(r_i d_i/d)(a/1)^i=0$. Thus $a/1$ is integral over $R_f$ in $B_f$ itself; no injectivity of $R	o A$ or $A	o A_{\mathfrak p}$ was used.

source.place: Tag 034K (lemma-integral-closure-stalks), proof: looking at denominators; explicit fraction calculation using Tag 07JZ (definition-localization-module).

proof.text: Every fraction $b/f^k\in B_f$ is a polynomial in $a/1$ with coefficients in $R_f$: write $b=\sum_i\varphi(b_i)a^i$, and then $b/f^k=\sum_i(b_i/f^k)(a/1)^i$. Conversely such polynomials belong to $B_f$. Therefore $B_f$ is exactly its $R_f$-subalgebra generated by the singleton $\{a/1\}$. Since this generator is integral by step 2, [lem-sc-finite-generated-integral-subring], with base $R_f$ and ambient algebra $B_f$, says that $B_f$ is a finite $R_f$-module.

source.place: Tag 034K (lemma-integral-closure-stalks), proof: S prime localized at f is finite; Tag 00GM (lemma-characterize-integral), proof for a singleton.

proof.text: For every prime $\mathfrak p$, steps 2 and 3 produce $f_{\mathfrak p}\notin\mathfrak p$ with $B_{f_{\mathfrak p}}$ finite over $R_{f_{\mathfrak p}}$. The principal opens $D(f_{\mathfrak p})$ therefore cover $\operatorname{Spec}R$. By the quasi-compactness clause of [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact], choose a finite subcover $D(f_1),\ldots,D(f_k)$. Its cover/unit-ideal clause gives $(f_1,\ldots,f_k)=R$.

source.place: Tag 034K (lemma-integral-closure-stalks), proof: finite subcover; Tag 00E8 (lemma-quasi-compact) and Tag 00E0 (lemma-Zariski-topology).

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-module-finite-of-localization-span] to the $R$-module $B$ and the elements $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ from step 4. Their ideal is the unit ideal, and every $B_{f_i}$ is a finite $R_{f_i}$-module by step 3. Consequently $B$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.

source.place: Tag 034K (lemma-integral-closure-stalks), proof: descent of finiteness; Tag 00EO (lemma-cover), part (2).

proof.text: The ring map $R\to B$ is finite by step 5. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral], its element $a\in B$ satisfies a monic polynomial over $R$. Applying the inclusion $B\subseteq A$ to that equation gives the same monic equation for the original $a\in A$. This proves the converse.

source.place: Tag 034K (lemma-integral-closure-stalks), last sentence; Tag 00GM (lemma-characterize-integral), reverse direction, via Tag 00GK (lemma-finite-is-integral).
